Time series data generally has a trend component, which is the general direction of where the time series is moving. For technical analysis on stocks, you want to understand if the trend is going up or down. You can also think about seasonality and cycles. Time series, by definition, has a sequence. This is very important because you cannot break the sequence of the data; the order is very important. If your data is sequential, you have a sequence from X1 all the way to XN. The difference with other data you're used to is that there's a sequence involved, meaning I cannot think of X1 and XN independently. They are all within a sequence. If I want to model them, I cannot assume they are independent. I need to ensure the structure is always intact. In contrast, with something like HDB resale data, X1 and X2 are just two separate independent samples of resale flats. It doesn't matter if I shuffle them. But for time series data, you cannot do that. You have to ensure the structure. The position is very important. For example, in the stock market, any data with a date attached loses its meaning if you shuffle it. The structure needs to be taken into account by any algorithms you are using. Cross-sectional data is what we've been working on all the time. If you're thinking in terms of a survey, predicting people's income, with a dataset of 1,000 people, it doesn't matter if I shuffle the rows because every row is independent. The model doesn't care about the sequence, so you do not need to model the sequence. You can jumble and split the data up, do train-test split, randomly shuffle; it doesn't matter because each data point is independent. Most typical supervised learning data is cross-sectional. Panel data is commonly used in econometrics. You can think of panel data as a dataset that has multiple variables tagged to a date. For example, three different stock prices with respect to the date. This combines time series and cross-sectional data, where you have multiple time series, and maybe another column categorizes them. Another example is sales data for different stores in Singapore. The rule of thumb is that if your data type has a timestamp or date, and this date is very important (without it, there's no context), then you are working with time series data. Cross-sectional data has individual independent instances, all independently collected. For panel data, you have a time series dataset that essentially has some categorization that allows you to break them into different portions, like sales data with date, sales value, store, and country. This will be a very common data type when you work with time series. The property of time series means that when we try to use algorithms to predict them, you have to treat them differently. You cannot take whatever you have learned so far and just apply it; it will not work. There will be a lot of issues because time series requires you to model the structure.

Time series decomposition is a methodology where, given a time series, you deconstruct it into different portions. You can break the time series up. There are many methods, including STL and the classical one, which we will teach. Other methods like X11 were created by different people. Time series has been around for a very long time; the classical decomposition came from 1920. The motivation for time series decomposition is either to forecast or to do some analysis. Decomposition helps you understand your time series clearer, rather than just visually. This is a more quantitative method. The idea is that a time series, at least from the classical method, can be decomposed mathematically into three additive portions: the trend, the seasonal component, and the residual (anything outside of your seasonal and trend). If you add these three together, you get back your observed time series. If you want to isolate and understand the trend, you look at the trend. If you want to capture the seasonality, the recurring cycle in the data, you do that. The remainder will be things outside of your trend and seasonal. That's how the classical method came about. In practice, people no longer use the classical method, but for pedagogy, it's important to have the intuition. The textbook introduces two methods: identifying if your time series is additive or multiplicative. Additive means the seasonal variation is independent and doesn't grow across time. Multiplicative means as time passes, the seasonal variation becomes larger and larger, proportional to the trend. It's important to identify additive or multiplicative because it affects the methodology used to break them down. There's also a transformation called Box-Cox. If you have a multiplicative model, you can perform a transformation to convert it back to additive if you want to use the additive method. You have to look at it visually to see if it works. Looking at examples, for an additive series, the cycle is consistent across time; it doesn't grow. For a multiplicative series, the variation of the cycle starts to become more and more, following the trend as time passes. This is a good sign it's multiplicative. For example, monthly demand in millions might be multiplicative if the cycle becomes stronger over time. Another example shows an additive time series where the variation did not change much. The mechanism for decomposition uses something called moving average or rolling average.

It penalizes the number of parameters to prevent overfitting, similar to how Ridge and Lasso regression add penalties. If the sample size is large, AIC is similar to leave-one-out cross-validation or walk-forward validation. AICC is an improvement over AIC, especially for smaller datasets, to avoid selecting overly complex models. BIC penalizes parameters even more heavily. For all three criteria, a lower value is better. AutoARIMA uses these to automatically select the best P and Q.

Autoregressive (AR) models use past values of the series to predict the next value, maintaining the sequential data structure. Moving Average (MA) models use past forecast errors. The 'I' in ARIMA stands for integrated, referring to the differencing needed to make the series stationary. ARIMA is well-established, good for short-term forecasting, and its structure is interpretable, though often used for prediction rather than deep interpretation. A key takeaway is that time series forecasting is a distinct field. While traditional ML can be used, it requires significant feature engineering to handle trends and maintain sequential structure. Hybrid approaches combining ML with traditional methods have shown strong performance. Other methods like ETS (Exponential Smoothing) and Prophet (a general additive model with Bayesian statistics) also exist. The best method depends on the specific dataset and requires empirical testing. Time series is a constantly developing field, so understanding the algorithms and questioning the methods is crucial.
